blocks.text: 1. Hierarchical Chunking

blocks.alt: A document splits into sections, then subsections, then paragraphs

blocks.text: Parent-Child Chunking introduced two tier chunking. Hierarchical Chunking extends that idea to arbitrarily many levels, splitting documents by their multi level structure.
It follows a document's own nested sections, subsections, and paragraphs.
2. From Two Levels To Many Levels
Parent child chunking used exactly two levels; many real documents have far more.
A book, manual, or report nests chapters, sections, and subsections several levels deep.
3. Documents Already Have Structure

blocks.alt: Headings form the existing document structure

blocks.text: Headings and subheadings already encode a document's own hierarchy.
Hierarchical chunking reuses that existing structure instead of inventing a new one.
4. Building A Tree Of Chunks

blocks.alt: A root document branches into a section, which leads to a paragraph leaf

blocks.text: Each heading level becomes a node, and its content becomes that node's chunk.
This produces a tree shaped structure that mirrors the document's own outline.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Document element","Tree structure"],"rows":[["Chapter heading","Top level node"],["Section and subsection headings","Nested child nodes below the chapter"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Navigating Up And Down The Tree

blocks.alt: A child node navigates to a parent node

blocks.text: A matched leaf node can pull in its parent section for broader context.
As with retrieving the parent instead in Parent-Child Chunking, the same upward lookup idea now applies across multiple levels.
6. Handling Documents Without Clear Headings

blocks.alt: No clear headings means falling back to flat chunking

blocks.text: Not every document carries clean, consistent heading markup.
As with detecting sentence boundaries in Sentence Chunking, structure detection can fail just as boundary detection can.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A document with inconsistent or missing heading tags produces a shallow or malformed tree. Falling back to recursive chunking is a sensible safeguard in that case.

blocks.text: 7. Hierarchical Chunking And Metadata

blocks.alt: A tree level gets attached as metadata

blocks.text: Each chunk can record its full path of ancestor headings.
A retrieved chunk knows exactly where it sits within the larger document.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A chunk carrying metadata like "Chapter 3, Section 2, Subsection 1" gives a retrieval system the ability to show a user exactly where an answer came from within a large document.

blocks.text: 8. Implementation Complexity
Building and maintaining a multi level tree takes more engineering effort than a flat list of chunks.
As with the storage and lookup overhead in Parent-Child Chunking, that same tradeoff scales up with each additional level.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Hierarchical Chunking Is Worth The Structure

blocks.alt: Documents with clear multi-level structure point toward hierarchical chunking

blocks.text: Long, deeply structured documents like manuals or textbooks benefit most.
Flat, unstructured content gains little from a hierarchy that does not actually exist in the source.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates building a chunk tree from headings and computing each chunk's ancestor path.

code.content:
document_outline = [
    {"level": 1, "heading": "Chapter 1: Introduction", "text": "This chapter introduces the system."},
    {"level": 2, "heading": "1.1 Background", "text": "The background section explains prior work."},
    {"level": 2, "heading": "1.2 Goals", "text": "The goals section lists project objectives."},
]

def build_ancestor_paths(outline):
    # building a tree of chunks
    stack = []
    chunks = []
    for node in outline:
        while stack and stack[-1]["level"] >= node["level"]:
            stack.pop()
        # hierarchical chunking and metadata
        path = [s["heading"] for s in stack] + [node["heading"]]
        chunks.append({"heading": node["heading"], "text": node["text"], "path": path})
        stack.append(node)
    return chunks

chunks = build_ancestor_paths(document_outline)
print("Chunks with ancestor paths:\n")
for chunk in chunks:
    print(f" {' > '.join(chunk['path'])}")
    print(f" text: {chunk['text']!r}\n")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows each subsection chunk carrying its full ancestor path back up to the chapter heading, giving retrieval systems full structural context.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Applying hierarchical chunking to documents that have no real internal heading structure.
Forgetting to record each chunk's ancestor path, losing the benefit of the tree structure entirely.
Having no fallback strategy when heading detection fails on a poorly formatted document.
Underestimating the added engineering complexity of maintaining a multi level tree.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Hierarchical chunking follows a document's own nested sections, subsections, and paragraphs.
It extends parent-child chunking's two tier idea to arbitrarily many levels.
Headings and subheadings already encode a document's hierarchy, which this strategy reuses directly.
Each heading level becomes a tree node, producing a structure that mirrors the document's outline.
A matched leaf node can pull in its parent section at any level for broader context.
Not every document has clean heading markup, so structure detection can fail and needs a fallback.
Each chunk can record its full ancestor path as metadata, showing exactly where it sits in the document.
Maintaining a multi level tree takes more engineering effort than a flat list of chunks.
